findings.title: Coalition, support, and disputed fabrication
findings.claim: The focus imagines humans and jinn gathered around a production task and gives the task reciprocal support. In 6:112 the same classes exchange embellished speech to mislead, while 25:4 preserves an allegation that other people helped fabricate the Quran. Set beside these wider passages, the support clause becomes a boundary on coordinated speech: aid and coalition can accompany misleading or alleged production, while the focus states that they still do not bring a Quranic counterpart.
findings.mechanism: The carriers are the human class, the gathering verb, and the supporter predicate in 17:88. The independent triggers are the shared task and part-to-part relation in the focus, 6:112's human-jinn mutual inspiration, and 25:4's reported assistance allegation. Their contact changes the tail from a bare measure of manpower into a wider dispute over what coordinated speech and assistance can produce.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see why the ayah names mutual support: coordinated speech and assistance are imaginable and appear in the wider evidence, yet this focus still denies that the coalition brings a likeness of the named Quran.
findings.containment: The human-jinn speakers in 6:112 are described as devils, not every human or jinn. The help in 25:4 is an allegation reported by opponents, not an established account. These limits keep both wider readings live without replacing the focus's hypothetical and denial.

epistemic.reason: The legacy reader walk is an unbound nomination. Exact target Arabic for 6:112 and 25:4, the focus surface, and registered focus branch facets ground the bounded relation, while the inference from those contexts remains qualified.

findings.title: Likeness beside inexhaustible words
findings.claim: The focus's likeness criterion meets a wider image of the Lord's words outlasting even a sea of ink and its like as further supply. This places the attempt to produce a Quranic counterpart beside a limit on finite resources, adding a scale of inexhaustibility to the coalition's failure.
findings.mechanism: The focus's mithl carrier asks for an equivalent of this Quran. In 18:109, the supplied Arabic uses the likeness expression for additional sea-as-ink supply, yet the sea would run out before the Lord's words. The contact shifts the reader's scale from the coalition alone to the finitude of what could write or supply those words.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the likeness question in a wider frame of finite means meeting an unexhausted discourse, alongside the focus's plain claim about a counterpart to this Quran.
findings.containment: In 18:109 the likeness refers to the sea or its ink supply, not to the Quran itself. The comparison adds a resource-limit image without claiming that the two verses have identical referents or that the Quran is literally the Lord's entire speech.

epistemic.reason: The reader-walk nomination is legacy_unbound; exact Arabic is supplied for 18:109, but the cross-verse scale comparison remains an inference.

findings.mechanism: The carrier is the focus's mithl phrase, which sets a Quranic whole as the comparison target. findings.reader_payoff: The reader can picture unity carried across portions and recitation, rather than assuming the comparison concerns only a text delivered all at once.
findings.containment: The focus still states that the coalition cannot bring its likeness. The supplied 17:106 text supports paced division; this finding does not claim that division weakens the whole or proves why it is inimitable.

findings.title: Gathering against a received text
findings.claim: The focus places human-jinn gathering and reciprocal support on the side of attempted production. In 75:17-19 the Quran's gathering and recitation, the instruction to follow its recitation, and its explanation are placed with divine agency; in 28:86 the Book is described as reaching the Messenger as mercy from his Lord, alongside a warning about becoming a supporter of disbelievers. This gives the focus's support clause a source-and-reception contrast in addition to its measure of collective effort.
findings.mechanism: The focus gathering verb is the carrier; the independent trigger is the 75:17-19 sequence assigning collection, recitation, and explanation to God. The supporter predicate is a second carrier; 28:86 joins the Book's arrival as mercy from the Lord to a warning using the supporter term. These contacts shift the challenge from how many agents help to the relation between collective production and a text received and operated by divine agency.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see that the challenge measures a coalition's capacity while the wider passages show a different relation for the Quran: it is received by a messenger and its gathering, recitation, and explanation are attributed to God.
findings.containment: The connections do not identify all details of their settings or prove an exclusive authorship theory. The focus's hypothetical coalition and its stated inability remain intact; the target morphology and lexical analyses for 28:86 are not supplied.

epistemic.reason: The candidate is a legacy_unbound nomination. Exact Arabic is supplied for 75:17-19 and 28:86, but their source-reception relation to this focus is interpretive and the 28:86 morphology is absent.

findings.title: The named jinn also receive the Quran
findings.claim: The focus names jinn among those imagined as possible producers of a likeness. In 72:1 a group of jinn reports hearing an astonishing Quran, and in 46:29-31 a group listens, identifies revealed guidance, and returns to call its people to answer. The focus's hidden class therefore has a wider role as receiver and transmitter of recitation alongside its place in the production challenge.
findings.mechanism: The carrier is the focus noun al-jinn. The independent triggers are the supplied 72:1 and 46:29-31 texts, which return through jinn hearing and responding to Quranic recitation. Contact shifts the scene from a single imagined coalition toward distinct relations between the hidden class and the text: possible production in the focus and reception or relay in the wider passages.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hold the jinn as both members of the proposed producing coalition and listeners who carry the recitation's call to others.
findings.containment: These passages describe particular groups, not every jinn. The supplied 46:32 text preserves refusal to answer, so reception is not universal and does not displace the focus's challenge.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch and exact Arabic for all cited target ayat are supplied. The connection records are nominations, and target morphology is not provided, so the cross-ayah role remains qualified.
